hazcom-overview.title: Why Hazard Communication Matters in Construction
hazcom-overview.content:
Construction workers regularly handle, use, store, or work near hazardous chemicals — often without recognizing the risk. Paints, adhesives, solvents, fuels, cleaners, concrete products, welding fumes, sealants, aerosols, and compressed gases can all create health, fire, explosion, or exposure hazards.

OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (HazCom, or Right-to-Know) gives workers the right to know about chemical hazards on the job. In construction, this means knowing:
- What hazardous chemicals are present and where they are used
- How those chemicals are labeled and where Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) are located
- What protective measures are required
- What to do in an emergency

OSHA coverage:
- Primary standard: 29 CFR 1910.1200 — Hazard Communication
- Construction application: 29 CFR 1926.59 — requirements are identical to 1910.1200

Hazard Communication exists to prevent chemical exposures from becoming injuries, illnesses, fires, or emergencies. Workers must be trained before working with or around hazardous chemicals, and that information must be available and understandable.

hazcom-three-sources.title: The Three Main Sources of Hazard Communication Information
hazcom-three-sources.content:
Under the Hazard Communication Standard, chemical hazard information is communicated in three main ways:

1. Container labels — provide quick, immediate hazard warnings right on the container. Read the label before opening, pouring, mixing, spraying, or applying any chemical.

2. Safety Data Sheets (SDSs) — provide detailed information about the chemical, its hazards, required precautions, PPE, first aid, storage, and spill response. SDSs must be readily accessible to employees during their work shifts.

3. Written Hazard Communication Program — explains how your employer manages chemical safety at the workplace: where SDSs are kept, how chemicals are inventoried, how employees are trained, and how chemical hazards are communicated between crews and subcontractors.

Key rules:
- Never use an unknown or unlabeled chemical
- Know where SDSs are located on your site before you need them
- The written program tells you the site-specific HAZCOM procedures

All three sources work together: the label gives immediate warnings, the SDS provides details, and the written program ties the whole system together.

safety-data-sheets.title: Safety Data Sheets
safety-data-sheets.content:
A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) is a detailed guide for safely using a chemical product. Manufacturers and distributors provide SDSs for all hazardous chemical products they sell. Employers must ensure SDSs are available to employees.

SDSs follow a standardized 16-section format based on the Globally Harmonized System (GHS):
- Section 1: Identification
- Section 2: Hazard(s) identification
- Section 4: First aid measures
- Section 5: Firefighting measures
- Section 6: Accidental release (spill response)
- Section 7: Handling and storage
- Section 8: Exposure controls and PPE
- Section 9: Physical and chemical properties
- Section 10–12: Stability, toxicology, ecological information

Before using a chemical, check the SDS for: hazard statements, required PPE, exposure controls, first aid instructions, spill response procedures, and storage requirements.

OSHA 1910.1200(g) requires SDSs to be readily accessible to employees during their work shift when they are in their work areas. The standardized format makes it easier to find information even across different manufacturers.

container-labels.title: Container Labels and Secondary Containers
container-labels.content:
Container labels provide quick, immediate information about a chemical's hazards. A GHS-compliant label includes: product identifier, signal word (Danger or Warning), hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements, and supplier information.

Key rules for labels:
- Always read the label before using a chemical
- Never remove or deface labels on incoming containers
- Never use chemicals from unlabeled containers
- Replace damaged or unreadable labels immediately
- Ensure the label matches the chemical inside

Secondary containers require special attention. A secondary container is any container a chemical is transferred into from its original container — spray bottles, buckets, smaller cans, or portable containers. Secondary containers MUST be properly labeled with chemical identity and hazard warnings per HAZCOM procedures, unless a very narrow immediate-use exception applies.

Example: A painter who pours thinner into an unlabeled spray bottle creates serious exposure and fire hazards for anyone else who picks it up. Proper labeling prevents misidentification and misuse.

OSHA 1910.1200(f) requires all containers of hazardous chemicals to be properly labeled.

chemical-hazard-classes.title: Common Classes of Hazardous Chemicals
chemical-hazard-classes.content:
Understanding chemical hazard classes helps workers recognize risks and choose the right precautions.

Toxic substances — interfere with normal body functions. May affect breathing, coordination, the nervous system, or organs. Some effects may be immediate (acute); others develop over time (chronic).

Corrosives and irritants — corrosives cause serious damage to skin, eyes, and tissues (acids and bases are common examples). Irritants cause redness, swelling, coughing, tearing, or temporary inflammation.

Flammables and combustibles — fuels, solvents, paints, thinners, adhesives, and aerosols. Flammable materials release vapors that ignite at relatively low temperatures. Vapors can travel to distant ignition sources — sparks, flames, hot surfaces — and ignite far from the original container.

Compressed and flammable gases — propane, acetylene, hydrogen, and others. Create fire, explosion, pressure, and oxygen-displacement hazards. Cylinders must be secured and stored correctly.

Carcinogens and suspected carcinogens — associated with cancer risk. May cause no immediate warning symptoms, making training, controls, and PPE especially critical.

Hazardous dusts and fumes — can be generated during cutting, grinding, welding, sanding, and demolition. Require engineering controls and/or respiratory protection.

routes-of-entry.title: Routes of Entry and Exposure Effects
routes-of-entry.content:
A chemical can only harm you if it enters or affects your body. The three main routes of entry are:

1. Skin or eye contact — chemicals may splash, spill, soak through clothing, or be absorbed through the skin. Eyes are especially vulnerable — vapors, dusts, and splashes can cause serious injury or permanent damage.

2. Inhalation — breathing in dusts, fumes, mists, vapors, or gases. Common in construction during spraying, mixing, cutting, welding, sanding, fueling, coating, or working in enclosed areas. The most common route of exposure on construction sites.

3. Ingestion — swallowing a chemical when contaminated hands touch food, drinks, cigarettes, chewing tobacco, or the face. Wash hands after chemical use and before eating or drinking.

Exposure effects depend on two key factors:
- Dose: how much of the chemical you are exposed to
- Duration: how long the exposure lasts

Acute effects happen quickly (burns, dizziness, coughing, nausea, eye irritation). Chronic effects develop over time after repeated or long-term exposure — these may not have immediate warning signs.

Report all chemical exposures and seek medical attention when required. Provide the SDS to medical personnel.

ppe-exposure-controls.title: PPE and Exposure Controls
ppe-exposure-controls.content:
Labels and SDSs identify the protective measures required for each chemical. Protection may include gloves, safety glasses, chemical goggles, face shields, protective clothing, aprons, ventilation, or respiratory protection.

PPE selection depends on: the specific chemical and its hazard class, the form of the chemical (liquid, vapor, dust), the amount used, the method of application, and the possible routes of entry.

Critical points:
- Not all gloves protect against all chemicals — chemical-resistant gloves must be matched to the specific substance using the SDS or compatibility chart
- Not all respirators protect against all vapors or particles — cartridges must be selected for the specific contaminant
- Cloth gloves may absorb chemicals instead of protecting against them
- Using the wrong PPE can create a false sense of security

PPE alone is not the only control. Use in combination with:
- Ventilation to control vapors, fumes, or gases
- Substitution (less hazardous alternative products)
- Proper storage and spill prevention
- Safer work practices (smaller quantities, enclosed systems)

Inspect PPE before each use. Replace damaged or contaminated PPE. Use respiratory protection only when trained, medically cleared, fit-tested, and authorized under the employer's respiratory program.

chemical-storage-handling.title: Safe Chemical Storage and Handling
chemical-storage-handling.content:
Proper storage and handling reduce the risk of exposure, fire, spills, and chemical reactions.

Storage guidelines:
- Keep containers closed when not in use (reduces spills, evaporation, vapor buildup, contamination)
- Store chemicals in organized, well-lit areas with labels remaining readable
- Separate incompatible chemicals — acids away from bases, oxidizers away from flammables
- Keep flammables and combustibles away from ignition sources
- Use approved containers and flammable storage cabinets where required
- Secure compressed gas cylinders upright at all times; never treat them like ordinary containers
- Maintain clear access to SDSs, eyewash stations, spill kits, and exits

Handling guidelines:
- Avoid awkward reaches, unstable shelves, and overfilled containers
- When transferring chemicals to secondary containers, label them immediately
- Ensure secondary containers are compatible with the material being transferred
- Use the smallest practical amount needed for the task

Example of what NOT to do: leaving a solvent container open near a temporary heater. Vapors build up and create a fire hazard. Keep containers closed and stored away from ignition sources.

spill-response.title: Spill Response and Chemical Emergencies
spill-response.content:
If a hazardous chemical leaks or spills, act quickly — but do not rush into danger.

Immediate priorities:
1. Protect people — warn others, evacuate the area if needed
2. Do NOT enter the spill area unless trained and authorized
3. Notify the appropriate supervisor, safety manager, or emergency personnel immediately
4. Control ignition sources if flammables are involved — but do NOT unplug electrical equipment or operate switches if vapors may be present (sparks can ignite vapors)

Cleanup responsibilities:
- Only trained, authorized, and properly equipped employees should clean up hazardous spills
- Review the SDS (Section 6 — Accidental Release Measures) before starting cleanup
- Use required PPE, appropriate spill control materials (absorbents, barriers, dikes), and proper disposal procedures
- Many chemicals and contaminated absorbents are regulated waste — do not throw them in ordinary trash

Eye splash emergency:
- Go IMMEDIATELY to an eyewash station
- Flush eyes for at least 15 minutes or per SDS instructions
- Notify supervision
- Seek medical attention — provide the SDS to medical personnel

Report all spills and exposures according to site procedures. A near miss or minor spill today can prevent a serious injury tomorrow.

employer-employee-responsibilities.title: Employee and Employer Responsibilities
employer-employee-responsibilities.content:
Hazard Communication works only when both employers and employees fulfill their roles.

Employee responsibilities:
- Read labels before using chemicals
- Know where SDSs are located and how to access them
- Follow the written Hazard Communication Program
- Use required PPE and exposure controls
- Label secondary containers per company procedures
- Keep containers closed when not in use
- Store chemicals only in approved areas
- Report unlabeled containers, missing SDSs, damaged labels, leaks, spills, and exposure symptoms
- Wash hands after chemical use and before eating, drinking, or smoking
- Ask questions before using unfamiliar chemicals

Employer and supervisor responsibilities:
- Maintain a written Hazard Communication Program
- Keep an accurate inventory of hazardous chemicals
- Ensure SDSs are readily accessible during all work shifts
- Ensure all containers are properly labeled
- Train employees before they work with or near hazardous chemicals
- Retrain when conditions, chemicals, or employee performance indicates a need
- Provide required PPE and exposure controls
- Communicate chemical hazards to subcontractors and affected workers
- Establish spill, exposure, storage, and disposal procedures
- Correct labeling, storage, or handling deficiencies promptly
